conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in. I’m Dr. Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how you’re adjusting to life after having your baby, and to make sure you’re getting any support you might need.

We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just ten questions about how you’ve felt over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and then we’ll talk through next steps together.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no clipboards or check-boxes. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start:  
In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Oh—yeah, I’ve still been laughing. My partner did that silly dance with the diaper on his head last night and I couldn’t stop giggling. So, no, laughing itself hasn’t felt hard; it’s actually one of the lighter moments in the day.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
That’s good to hear. What about looking forward with enjoyment to things—have you still been able to get excited about little outings or small pleasures, or has that enthusiasm slipped away lately.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I still get excited about stuff—like yesterday I was really looking forward to our afternoon walk to the coffee shop. It’s a tiny outing, but it feels like a win when I actually make it there with the stroller.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her outfit, I might think, “Well, maybe I should’ve burped her longer,” but I don’t dwell on it. Stuff just happens with babies—I figure it out and move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like, the other night I suddenly worried her breathing sounded different—even though she was peacefully asleep and totally fine. It lasted a few minutes, then I reminded myself she’s healthy, and I calmed down. It’s not constant, just little spurts that pass pretty quickly.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t had any sudden panic or felt scared out of the blue—just those quick worries about the baby, but they never turn into a real scared or panicky feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me
Not really—most days feel manageable. If she’s fussy or the laundry piles up I’ll think “okay, this is a lot,” but I just tackle one thing at a time. Overall I still feel like I’m coping fine.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, that hasn’t happened. I’ve been sleeping pretty well—usually get a four-hour stretch, then up for a quick feed, and back to sleep for another few hours. My mood hasn’t interfered with that at all.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt sad or miserable. Tired sometimes, sure, but not down or weepy—most moments I’d describe as “pretty okay,” even happy when she smiles.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried from feeling unhappy. Maybe a tear or two when I was super tired a few nights ago, but it was more exhaustion than sadness, and it passed quickly.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. That hasn’t crossed my mind—no thoughts like that.

You shared that the past week has felt largely manageable and even joyful-<quote>I couldn't stop giggling</quote> at your partner's antics, and you still look forward to simple outings like pushing the stroller to the coffee shop. You described only fleeting worries about the baby's breathing that pass quickly, and you're sleeping in good stretches. You denied persistent sadness, crying spells, guilt, or thoughts of self-harm, noting instead that most moments feel <quote>pretty okay</quote>.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 3, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Her specific example of sudden, brief, unprovoked worry about the baby's breathing maps to the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 3 falls well below the 9-point threshold where <med>postpartum depression</med> becomes possible. You endorsed only one item (<sym>brief unexplained worry</sym>) at the mild level; all other mood, pleasure, coping, sleep, and self-harm items were scored zero. This pattern does not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which requires ≥5 symptoms (including low mood or anhedonia) most of the day for ≥2 weeks. Your report of maintained enjoyment, laughter, and good sleep further supports a low-risk picture. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue enjoying daily outings and share any new emotional changes at your next postpartum visit
2. Re-screen with EPDS if low mood, persistent worry, or sleep-mood links develop
3. Keep your support network involved-family, friends, or new-parent groups can buffer normal postpartum stress
4. Practise quick relaxation techniques (deep breathing, grounding) for the occasional worry spike
5. Seek immediate care if you ever notice worsening mood, panic episodes, or thoughts of self-harm
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 3: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening  
Source: Self-report on 10-item EPDS-analogue questionnaire  

<sym>Symptoms endorsed:</sym>  
- Transient, situational worries about infant wellbeing (Q4) – no generalised or panic-level anxiety (Q5)  
- No persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep-mood linkage, crying spells, or self-harm ideation  

<sym>Symptoms denied:</sym>  
- Loss of pleasure or motivation (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (Q3)  
- Feeling overwhelmed or unable to cope (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)  
- Sad/miserable affect (Q8)  
- Unhappy crying (Q9)  
- Self-harm thoughts (Q10)  

Clinical impression:  
No indicators meeting screening threshold for probable postpartum depression or anxiety disorder at this time. Patient demonstrates positive coping, intact enjoyment, and normative new-parent concerns. Continue routine perinatal support; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
